s1.p1:
Now we'll learn how to work with another very important type of data: **⟦f0⟧**.
Our entire "JS universe" is based on functions.

**Functions are a reference type of data.**.

This means that after declaring a function, we will have a variable in our hands that will be a reference to the function.
s1.p2: When someone is sick, a doctor will be called, when there are problems with water supply or sewerage, a plumber will be called, and when there are problems with wiring in the house, we call an electrician. It's good that there are doctors, plumbers and electricians. Please note that they do not live in our house and do not do their work all the time. Otherwise, there would be hell in our house, crowds of people who are doing something all the time... No, no, we call them only when the need arises. They come, do their job and leave. But we still have a phone or another way to call them if the problem arises again.
s1.p5: Each function can be called when the need arises.
s1.p6: Let's first learn how to call them.

s2.p1: We have a lot of built-in functions and there are also functions that the browser provides us.
s2.p2: A function call consists of two parts: the function name and parentheses following the function name, in which **arguments** can be passed, i.e. some data that the function will use in its work.
s2.p3: There are functions that do not require passing arguments when called. In this case, you can call such a function with empty parentheses, but parentheses are required. If you pass arguments to such a function, it will simply ignore them because they are not needed for it to work. If you pass more arguments than necessary, unnecessary arguments will be discarded.

s6.p1: We have already learnt how to call functions. It's time to learn how to create them, or more precisely, how to declare functions.
s6.p2: Exactly declare, because our goal is not to immediately call a function where we have declared it.
s6.p3: In order to properly declare a function, we need to understand how a function differs from all other data types.
s6.p4: Firstly, a function contains the code that will be executed when the function is called.
s6.p5: This code is placed in curly braces and is called the **body of the function**.

s6.p9: No, we obviously need something else.
s6.p10: For example, we need the code to be saved under some name, but not executed in the place where it appeared.
s6.p11: So that we can run that code later, when we need to, to execute it. Not immediately, but sometime later.

s7.p1: Let's go back to the fact that parentheses are required when declaring a function.
s7.p2: When calling a function, parentheses are also required.
s7.p3: Obviously, parentheses play an important role here.
s7.p4: Recall how parentheses can be used when calling a function: we use them to pass **arguments** to the function. I.e. we place some data to parentheses for the function to use this data at runtime.
s7.p5: Ok, but how does the function receive this data?
s7.p6: Arguments have to be saved somewhere, and function needs a reference to them to operate with.
s7.p7: And where do we store the data? Well, not in drawers, and not in basins, and not in pots.
s7.p9: That is, in order to accept the arguments passed when calling a function, we need to prepare the variables where these data (arguments) will be placed beforehand.
s7.p10: And somehow it is self-evident that we should place the names of these variables to the same place where the arguments will be received later.
s7.p13: Thus, when declaring a function, we use parentheses to list there the names of variables that we will use for calculations in the body of the function.
s7.p14: These variables are called **formal parameters** of the function.
s7.p15: These variables have no values at the time the function is declared.
s7.p16: When the function is called, **arguments** will be listed in parentheses, which will become the values of the formal parameters at this moment.
s7.p17: That is, each time we call the function, we can pass different arguments to it, thus getting different results.
